title: Acute Stroke: Reperfuse Fast, Then Prevent the Next Event
bottomLine: A new disabling focal neurologic deficit is an acute-stroke emergency. Establish last-known-well, check glucose, activate a stroke-capable pathway and obtain immediate brain plus vascular imaging so hemorrhage is excluded and thrombolysis/endovascular-thrombectomy eligibility can be determined without avoidable delay; after stabilization, secondary prevention must target the actual stroke mechanism.
recognize: Sudden unilateral weakness or numbness, aphasia/dysarthria, visual-field loss, neglect, ataxia, gaze deviation or another abrupt focal deficit can represent acute stroke even when pain is absent.

Posterior-circulation stroke may present with severe gait/truncal ataxia, diplopia, dysarthria, vertigo or reduced consciousness and can be missed when the examination focuses only on FAST-type anterior-circulation signs.

A normal initial noncontrast CT excludes neither early ischemia nor large-vessel occlusion; its immediate jobs include hemorrhage assessment and support for reperfusion decision-making with vascular imaging.
differentiate: Hypoglycemia, seizure/postictal deficit, migraine aura and selected toxic/metabolic or functional syndromes can mimic stroke, but a plausible acute focal syndrome is not observed in clinic while those alternatives are leisurely excluded.
Ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke require different antithrombotic/reperfusion pathways; do not give antiplatelet therapy before intracranial hemorrhage has been excluded.
TIA is transient focal dysfunction with high early recurrence risk, but a persistent disabling deficit belongs to the acute stroke/reperfusion pathway rather than a routine outpatient TIA workup.
assessment: Document symptom onset or last-known-well, baseline function, exact neurologic deficits, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and last dose, recent surgery/bleeding/trauma, pregnancy/postpartum status and major comorbidity while ABCs are stabilized.

Check point-of-care glucose promptly and assess blood pressure, oxygenation, temperature, cardiac rhythm and swallowing risk without allowing a prolonged general examination to delay stroke-team activation or imaging.

Use a standardized stroke-severity assessment in the acute-care pathway while recognizing that some disabling posterior, language or visual deficits can be clinically important despite a modest numeric score.
workup: For potentially reperfusion-eligible ischemic stroke, obtain immediate noncontrast brain imaging plus head/neck vascular imaging according to the stroke-capable centre pathway; current Canadian recommendations use rapid CTA-based assessment and advanced imaging selectively for later-window/tissue-based EVT selection.
Obtain acute laboratory testing and ECG/rhythm information needed for treatment safety and mechanism evaluation, but do not delay reperfusion solely for nonessential test results.

After the emergency phase, investigate mechanism with vascular imaging, cardiac/rhythm assessment and other targeted studies so secondary prevention is etiology-specific rather than a generic medication bundle.
management: Activate EMS/code-stroke transfer immediately and involve stroke expertise on-site or through telestroke. Eligible patients should receive IV thrombolysis as soon as possible; patients meeting current imaging/clinical criteria should proceed to endovascular-thrombectomy evaluation without waiting to see whether thrombolysis produces clinical improvement.

Provide stroke-unit care after reperfusion/diagnosis, including physiologic monitoring, early complication prevention, swallowing assessment before routine oral intake/medications, mobilization/rehabilitation planning and management of cerebral edema, hemorrhagic transformation, seizures or other complications when they arise.

Build secondary prevention from mechanism: antiplatelet therapy for appropriate non-cardioembolic disease, anticoagulation for atrial-fibrillation/cardioembolic indications when timing is safe, vascular risk treatment, smoking support, lipid/BP/diabetes management, carotid or other vascular intervention when indicated, and rehabilitation/return-to-function planning.
medicationSafety: Do not give antiplatelet therapy during the first 24 hours after IV thrombolysis; repeat brain imaging must exclude secondary hemorrhage before antiplatelet initiation according to the acute stroke pathway.

Current Canadian guidance does not support routine IV thrombolysis in a patient actively taking a DOAC without specialized assessment; provide the exact anticoagulant, dose and last-dose timing to the stroke team rather than assuming all anticoagulation has the same implication.
Avoid reflex blood-pressure normalization: acute BP targets depend on reperfusion candidacy, hemorrhage versus ischemia and other clinical factors and belong to the validated acute-stroke protocol.
redFlags: Any new persistent focal neurologic deficit
Reduced consciousness, severe headache/vomiting or suspected intracranial hemorrhage
Large-vessel-occlusion features or disabling posterior-circulation syndrome
Neurologic deterioration after thrombolysis or EVT
Acute stroke during pregnancy/postpartum or while anticoagulated
Progressive cerebral edema, airway compromise or recurrent seizure
counselling: Teach the patient/family that stroke treatment is time- and tissue-sensitive: call emergency services for new focal symptoms rather than driving to clinic or waiting to see whether symptoms resolve.

Before discharge, explain the identified stroke mechanism, each prevention medication/intervention, rehabilitation plan, recurrence warning signs, driving/work considerations and responsibility for pending rhythm/vascular investigations using teach-back.
followUp: Use a closed-loop transition to stroke prevention/primary care/rehabilitation, including medication reconciliation and completion of mechanism-specific investigations such as prolonged rhythm monitoring when indicated.

Reassess functional recovery, cognition/mood, swallowing/nutrition, falls, recurrence symptoms, treatment tolerability and vascular risk rather than limiting follow-up to blood pressure or antithrombotic refills.
examTrap: Waiting for MRI or a second outpatient examination before activating acute stroke care—or giving aspirin before hemorrhage is excluded because the focal deficit 'looks ischemic'.
oneLinePearl: Acute stroke is imaging-to-reperfusion first, mechanism-to-prevention second.
